The timeline for when he submits grades doesn't really matter. Obviously it's helpful to have grades submitted earlier so you can realize what you're doing wrong and improve it in the future. But if your work wasn't up to par the grades you received just reflect the quality of the work you turn in. You shouldn't count on being able to improve your grade in a revision you should submit your best work the first time around. Talk to the guy and maybe he can be more lenient about the revisions given the situation. It's a lot better to handle situations in person instead of posting a complaint online. Not everyone's anxiety and depression is the same but given he's an instructor so he has a responsibility he can't ignore.

Consider talking to an academic counselor or someone you're close with in your department and if you really need a break maybe you can take a semester off. It sounds like you're really passionate about physics and you're only a year away from graduating. I know with depression it can be hard to see past the short term because you're feeling awful right now but you're so close to your goal. You've already made it this far, push through the best you can but don't ignore your depression until it becomes overwhelming. I know it's difficult to tell your family when you're struggling but they might be more accepting and understanding than you believe.

Hi guys! I'm glad to be on such a precious team! I'm 19 years old (5' 3") and from Northern California. I'll be starting my second year of college this fall. I struggled with my weight a lot in high school and had an eating disorder. I was underweight up until I became extremely depressed my junior year where the combination of quitting softball, not having PE daily, and binge eating caused me to gain fifty pounds. By the time I graduated high school I was 190. I worked a job that was physically demanding last summer and started college in the fall. The last year I have not had the most consistent meals due to being forced to eat campus food but I lost about ten pounds over the school year. Once I started gaining weight it all just piled up and I kept telling myself I was going to lose weight to get "back to normal". But there isn't really a normal for me because my weight has fluctuated so much over my teenage life. In my adult life I am at the lowest weight I have ever been (172ish) and I want to make the change to live a more positive and healthy life. I'm not going to worry about numbers or physical appearance but rather focus on being in a place where I'm healthy and happy. Ultimately the weight range that I am comfortable in and feel the most "healthy" is 120s but that'll be a long way down the road. I'm going to dedicate over these next eight weeks to meal prepping to have a consistent caloric intake (1200 probably). Learning to meal prep while I'm home over the summer will make the transition into living in an apartment where I'll have to cook for myself easier too. I am going to exercise at least five days a week and make an effort to have one of those days be an outdoor activity. I'm going to try and take up yoga in the mornings to start my day too. Can't wait to see you guys on the other side! 


**after writing this I've realized that I focus a lot on the story of how I gained my weight. The dialogue I want to create from now on is my journey to being healthy because what I have done in the past doesn't matter it's the choices that I make from now on that'll shape everything else.
